children.text: A flat island floating in Lamon Bay off Mauban, Quezon, known for the vast sandy flats and mangrove forest that appear when the sea pulls back hundreds of meters at low tide. Electricity and amenities are basic, but that same quiet has made it a favorite weekend camping and sunrise getaway for travelers from Manila.

Cagbalete Island is an island of about 16–17 square kilometers in Lamon Bay, which opens onto the Pacific off Mauban in Quezon province on Luzon's east coast. It falls administratively under Mauban, and it's under an hour from Mauban port by banca (outrigger boat). Reachable from Manila in half a day by bus and boat, it has remained a steady favorite for a weekend, two-day-one-night island getaway.

This island's defining trait is its tidal range. The whole island sits just a few meters above sea level and the water offshore is shallow, so at low tide the sea retreats hundreds of meters, exposing a cream-colored sand flat rippled with wave patterns. At high tide you swim in a calm jade-colored sea, and at low tide you walk across that same seabed — two completely different scenes in a single day.

Along the beach, agoho (ironwood) trees and coconut palms cast shade, and a broad mangrove forest grows at the river mouth inland. Sabang, a fishing village on the island's west side, is the gateway where boats land, while most resorts where travelers stay are scattered along the east and southeast beaches, facing the sunrise.
There are no big resorts or busy streets. Electricity, which long depended on resort generators, has been supplied around the clock since Meralco's solar-and-battery microgrid went into operation in
December 2025

, but capacity is still being expanded and conditions differ from resort to resort. It suits travelers who are willing to put up with inconvenience to pitch a tent or rest in a simple hut to the sound of the waves, and groups such as university clubs or friends who want to camp together. If you expect comfortable hotels and flashy activities, you may be disappointed.

At low tide the sea pulls back far into the distance, revealing an endless expanse of ripple-marked sand flats and small tide pools. Walking barefoot, you'll easily spot crabs, shells, and starfish, and the sky-reflecting tide pools are a popular photo spot. Be sure to check the tide table before you go.
The east beach, where the resorts cluster, faces the Pacific, making for beautiful sunrises. Head out to the beach around
and you can watch the sun rise beyond the bancas.

Mangroves grow thick at the river mouth inland, forming small channels. Rent a kayak from your resort or book a banca tour and paddle in along the channels at high tide. There are plenty of water birds and small fish.
Cagbalete is one of the Philippines' top beach-camping spots. Pay a resort about
for a tent site and you can pitch your tent in the shade of the trees; renting a tent is also an option.

You can charter a banca for a short island-hopping trip around the Yang-in sandbar and a fish sanctuary near the island. Which spots are reachable depends on the tide, so coordinate timing with your boatman first.

blocks.title: Swimming and snorkeling at high tide

children.text: With shallow water and calm waves, high tide is good for kids to play in the water too. It's not a place with vivid coral reefs, but you can spot seagrass and small fish on the shallow bottom.
Most resorts either lend out a grill or offer a paluto service, cooking food you bring. With so little light on the island, you can hope to see the Milky Way on a clear night.

Scheduled banca times change with the season and passenger numbers, so it's worth confirming the round-trip boat schedule when you book your resort. If you have extra time, extend the trip to three days, two nights and add a stop in Lucban or Tayabas.

The eastern Quezon coast, where Cagbalete sits, has a slightly different season from western Philippines. Facing the Pacific,
November–February
brings frequent rain and high waves from the northeast monsoon (Amihan), causing occasional boat cancellations.
March–May
, by contrast, is the best time, with little rain and a calm sea, though midday temperatures climb to
and shaded camping spots fill up quickly.
June–October

is the wet season and typhoon season, and this area is directly affected when typhoons enter eastern Luzon. Boats don't sail when the Philippine Coast Guard issues a small-craft warning, so be sure to check PAGASA forecasts. Holy Week (the week before Easter) and summer-break weekends draw crowds of campers, so tent sites and huts sell out early — book ahead. If you want to see the low-tide sand flats, check the tide table for a daytime low tide when choosing your dates.

Accommodation consists entirely of small resorts on the island's east and southeast beaches. Long-running ones such as Villa Cleofas, MVT Santoniño Resort, and Pansacola Beach Resort are typical, and all focus on tent spots and fan-cooled huts, with only a few air-conditioned rooms. Tent spots run about
a night and huts about

. Electricity has improved with the microgrid, but supply hours may differ by resort, and the water is groundwater that can taste salty. On peak-season weekends always book ahead, and when you do, ask about power supply hours and how meals are handled.

With almost no restaurants on the island, most visitors use the resort restaurant, or bring meat and seafood bought at Mauban market to grill themselves after renting a grill, or pay a cooking fee to have it prepared. Mauban market sells fish, squid, and crab caught in Lamon Bay at low prices. It's best to try Quezon specialties like Lucban longganisa and pancit habhab in Lucban or Lucena on the way back. Bring plenty of drinking water, snacks, and ice from Mauban.
Check the tide table before setting your travel dates. You need a daytime low tide to see the sand flats, and a daytime high tide for proper swimming.
There's no ATM on the island, and cards and digital payments don't work well either. Bring cash for boat fare, lodging, and meals.
Phone signal is weak and charging time is limited, so bring a power bank and a flashlight.
Many resorts prohibit high-power devices like rice cookers, electric kettles, and hair dryers.
It's more economical to buy drinking water in Mauban. Shops on the island have limited selection and higher prices.
The sand flats have shells and sharp stones at low tide, so wear aqua shoes.
If you're camping, bring mosquito repellent, a mat, and a light blanket. The pre-dawn sea breeze is cooler than you'd expect.
If you miss the afternoon boat on your departure day, you may have to stay on the island until the next day. Arrive at Sabang port
1 hour
before departure.
If you walk far out at low tide and the tide comes back in quickly, you can get stranded or fall into a deep channel. Check the tide times and head back to the beach before the tide starts coming in.
If a small-craft or typhoon warning is issued, boats stop running and you could be stranded on the island, so build a buffer day into your schedule after your planned return date.
Wear a life vest when riding a banca, and avoid boats that carry more passengers than their capacity.
The shallow water can have sea urchins and jellyfish, so a rash guard and aqua shoes are safer.
Don't take shells or starfish from the mangroves or beach, and carry all your trash back out with you.
There's no hospital on the island, and an emergency means traveling to Mauban by boat, so bring a basic first-aid kit.
